judge.label: LLM rubric score, fresh-context judge, self-assessed — not human QA.
judge.independence_caveat: This judge is a different model family and a fresh context: it saw only the judge prompt, the rubric and the lesson. It did not direct the project and did not author anything in it. It is still a language model scoring a language model's output, so the label applies: not human QA.

notes.bilingual_quality: Mostly solid Arabic, but several spots read as translated or machine-adjacent: «الاتصال بالمنتهي» is an unclear rendering of 'contacting the person whose shift ended'; «وعد بإنجاز فعل معين» is stiff for 'complete a specific action'; «من المحتمل أن تكون الشبكة معطلة» is a calque of English 'probably' where «غالبًا» is the natural choice; «الطلب وصل أولًا» is an anglicised sequencing cue. Also a parity slip: the Arabic worked-example prompt says the customer was promised a reply while the English says the customer asked for one. Terminology itself is consistent throughout.

verdict_notes: The knowledge checks are the strongest part — every distractor is a documented real-world failure mode (arrival-order, tidiness-by-ticket-number, overcorrection-by-deletion) and the feedback names the misconception rather than restating the stem. The weakest part is the Arabic: understandable and consistent in terminology, but with enough translated phrasing and one genuinely unclear rendering (الاتصال بالمنتهي) that it sits at 'accurate, occasionally stiff' rather than natural. Everything else is competent, lean, and aligned; the lesson would pass on the strength of its practice blocks.
